theme: Christian freedom; the fruit of the Spirit; the new creation
readingInstruction: Read Galatians 5:1-6:18. Paul moves from the doctrine of freedom to its practice. Notice the contrast between flesh and Spirit, the fruit of the Spirit, and the closing summary about the cross and new creation.
settingTheScene: Paul has argued that we are justified by faith, not law. But does this freedom lead to a life of license? The opposite error was also a danger. In chapters 5 and 6, Paul shows how freedom works: we are called to freedom, but we use it to serve others in love, and we live by the Spirit who produces holiness. This is one of the best summaries of the Christian life in the New Testament.
observation: “For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery” (5:1).
“For you were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another” (5:13).
“But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh” (5:16).
“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control; against such things there is no law” (5:22-23).
“Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (6:2).
“And let us not grow weary of doing good, for in due season we will reap, if we do not give up” (6:9).
“Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world” (6:14).
“For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (6:15).
interpretation:
“For freedom Christ has set us free; stand firm therefore, and do not submit again to a yoke of slavery.” Paul warns that if the Galatians accept circumcision as a means of righteousness, Christ will be of no advantage to them, and they are obligated to keep the whole law. “You are severed from Christ, you who would be justified by the law; you have fallen away from grace.” In Christ Jesus, what counts is “faith working through love.”

Then the other danger: “You were called to freedom, brothers. Only do not use your freedom as an opportunity for the flesh, but through love serve one another. For the whole law is fulfilled in one word: You shall love your neighbor as yourself.” Freedom from the law is not freedom from love. It is freedom to love. “But if you bite and devour one another, watch out that you are not consumed by one another.”

The solution is the Spirit. “Walk by the Spirit, and you will not gratify the desires of the flesh. For the desires of the flesh are against the Spirit, and the desires of the Spirit are against the flesh, for these are opposed to each other, to keep you from doing the things you want to do.” This is the war within every believer. The “works of the flesh” are obvious: sexual immorality, impurity, sensuality, idolatry, sorcery, enmity, strife, jealousy, fits of anger, rivalries, dissensions, divisions, envy, drunkenness, orgies. Those who do such things will not inherit the kingdom of God. Notice how many involve relationships.

In contrast, “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faithfulness, gentleness, self-control.” The singular “fruit” suggests one character with nine facets. It is the character of Christ. It grows; it is not manufactured. We cannot produce fruit by effort alone, but by abiding. And “those who belong to Christ Jesus have crucified the flesh with its passions and desires. If we live by the Spirit, let us also keep in step with the Spirit.”

Chapter 6 gives practical instructions: restore gently someone caught in a transgression, watching yourself lest you too be tempted. “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ.” Each must also bear his own load (the daily responsibility). Share good things with those who teach. “Do not be deceived: God is not mocked, for whatever one sows, that will he also reap.” Sowing to the Spirit leads to eternal life. “Let us not grow weary of doing good.”

Paul takes the pen in his own hand to write the closing in large letters. His boast is not in circumcision or any achievement. “Far be it from me to boast except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, by which the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world. For neither circumcision counts for anything, nor uncircumcision, but a new creation.” The cross is the center, and the new creation is the goal. “Peace and mercy be upon all who walk by this rule, upon the Israel of God.” Interpreters differ about whether “the Israel of God” means the church, composed of Jews and Gentiles, or believing Jews within the church. In a progressive covenantal reading, it points to the one people of God, united in Christ.
connection: Romans 6 to 8 expands the same themes of freedom and the Spirit. Leviticus 19:18 is quoted in 5:14. John 15:1-17 shows fruit through abiding. Ephesians 4:1-6:20 and Colossians 3:1-17 give related moral teaching. Matthew 7:15-20 says a tree is known by its fruit. 2 Corinthians 5:17 speaks of new creation. Isaiah 65:17 and Revelation 21:5 promise all things new. Hebrews 12:1 calls us to lay aside weights. 1 Corinthians 2:2 shows Paul’s focus on the cross.
application:
Choose one fruit of the Spirit that you most need this week. Ask for it, and look for a place to practice it.

Ask whom you can help carry a burden. Do it quietly.

Put your name in 6:14. What do you boast in besides the cross?
prayerPrompts: Thank Jesus for setting you free, and ask him to keep you from returning to slavery.
Ask the Spirit to produce his fruit in you.
Tell him which fruit you most need.
